sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the connection between the two interpretations of "beloved friends" and the request for joy in Chochmah and Binah.

translations.translation: And one may add,
that the connection of the two interpretations of "beloved friends"
[for the primary interpretation is that "beloved friends" refers to Chochmah and Binah, as explained at length in the maamar,
except that there is another interpretation that it refers
(also)
to Zeir Anpin and Nukvah],
is also in the matter of "rejoice, You will rejoice," etc.
For this request that joy be drawn into Chochmah and Binah
(the primary interpretation of "beloved friends"),
even though they already have joy and delight in and of themselves,
is that a joy more elevated than the joy they have from their own essence be drawn into them
(as will be explained at length below).
And the reason that it is necessary to draw into them additional joy is so that through this there will be revelation in Zeir Anpin and Nukvah
(the second interpretation of "beloved friends")20.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section discusses that serving God must be with joy, yet there are many levels of joy, from limited joy to essential joy.

translations.translation: And the explanation is,
that the service of God must be with joy, as it is written21
"Serve God with joy," and it is written22
"Because you did not serve God your God with joy and goodness of heart."
And since a person must serve God in all his affairs,
and "all your deeds shall be for the sake of Heaven"23
and
(even more so24)
"in all your ways know Him"25,
to the extent that this
(the service of God)
is the purpose of all his creation, as our Sages said26
"I was not created except to serve my Creator,"
it follows that he must always be in a state of joy.
However, there are different levels of joy.
For there are specific places that are places of joy,
such as "the building of joy"27.
And so it is with regard to time,
for there are specific times
(festivals)
that are "appointed times for joy"28.
And even within them themselves there are different levels,
such as the festival of Sukkot, which is
(also)
"the time of our joy"29.
And especially in the Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing, of which "whoever has not seen the Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing has never seen joy in his life"30,
where they would dance with torches of light31,
for "torches of light" are the aspect of Chochmah, and the matter of the dancing
(with the torches)
is the drawing down
(of the aspect of Chochmah)
into Binah
[And even within this joy itself there are different levels,
for they would not perform it etc. except the great sages of Israel etc., and all the people etc. would come to see and hear32].
And especially on Simchat Torah, for the joy of Simchat Torah is more elevated even than the joy of the Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing, as stated in Likkutei Torah33,
to the extent that the name of this day
(for the name of every thing indicates its matter and vitality34)
is "Simchat Torah"35.
From all this it is understood that there are many, many levels of joy.
And they are generally divided into two aspects36.
Joy that is composite in some thing
(such as joy stemming from intellectual comprehension and the like),
for this joy is in the revealed faculties and is in the category of limitation,
and essential joy, which is primarily in the essence of the soul,
which is above the category of limitation.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that joy breaks boundaries, both those of habit and those of innate nature, because it stems from the soul's essence which is beyond limitation.

translations.translation: And this will be understood according to what is explained in the maamar there37
that the nature of joy is to break boundaries,
that is, every definition and limitation in the soul.
And there he explains two modes of this.
The first mode,
that joy breaks the boundaries that were made in a person due to his having become accustomed to them,
even though these boundaries have become like a nature for him
(for habit becomes a second nature38),
and the second mode,
that joy has the power to break even the boundaries of his innate nature,
to the extent that joy has the power to overturn them and change them from one extreme to the opposite extreme,
and this means,
that joy breaking the boundaries of his innate nature is not only that those traits that were ingrained in the person are in abundance and intensification beyond their measure,
but that through joy a change is also made in the nature of his traits, from one extreme to the opposite extreme.
For example, one who is extremely miserly and stingy by his innate nature,
behold, at a time of joy,
when he rejoices with very great joy,
his heart will be completely overturned from his previous nature and he will become extremely generous and benevolent,
like one who is generous and benevolent by nature,
to the extent that he acts kindly even with his enemy,
and one might say even to his enemy according to Torah law39.
And behold, even in the first mode, where joy breaks a boundary stemming from habit,
explanation is needed,
for since every habit becomes a nature,
even if it is only a second nature,
it would seemingly require a great amount of time and effort to change this nature little by little,
so how can joy have the power to change it in an instant?
And all the more so in the second mode,
one must understand,
how can joy have the power to break the boundaries of his innate nature,
to the extent that it has the power to change and overturn his nature from one extreme to the opposite extreme?
And the explanation is
(as explained in the maamar there40),
that joy breaking boundaries
(even in the first mode,
and certainly in the second mode)
is specifically with such joy that reaches the essence of the soul,
which is above the revealed faculties.
For since the essence of the soul is above the category of limitation
(because it is connected with the Awtsmoos),
therefore,
joy that stems from the essence of the soul
breaks all definitions and limitations.
